claims.text: Plastic deformation in the quaternary equiatomic FCC HEA under uniaxial tension will be governed by dislocation glide on {111} planes.
Deformation twins and stacking faults will contribute to plastic deformation in the quaternary alloy.
Yield strength will be dominated by solid-solution strengthening caused by severe lattice distortion.
At low strain rates and moderate temperatures, yield strength will become insensitive to strain rate.
Strain-rate insensitivity will arise from thermally activated cross-slip and stacking-fault-energy-mediated twin nucleation rather than dislocation climb.
Strain-rate insensitivity is expected above approximately 0.3 Tm or at very low strain rates where cross-slip or diffusion-assisted processes dominate.
An annealed quaternary FCC HEA may retain a high dislocation density inherited from synthesis.
Transient HCP phase may form at twin boundaries or other high-stress regions.
High configurational entropy produces severe lattice distortion that impedes dislocation motion.
Severe lattice distortion promotes twinning as a secondary mode for accommodating strain.
A transition from dislocation glide to an FCC-to-HCP transformation will occur at cryogenic temperatures or high strain rates because the effective stacking-fault energy is lowered by stress.
The quaternary alloy will exhibit high yield strength together with significant ductility.
The tensile stress-strain curve will exhibit a continuous strain-hardening regime.
At 77 K, deformation twinning will make a significant contribution to plasticity.
At 77 K, an FCC-to-HCP transformation may occur at twin boundaries.
Above 300 K and at low strain rates, yield strength will plateau because cross-slip becomes the rate-limiting step.
High dislocation density and twin boundaries will serve as preferential corrosion-initiation sites and reduce corrosion resistance relative to a defect-free single crystal.
Conventional FCC Ni and Cu deform predominantly by dislocation glide, exhibit minimal twinning, and have comparatively weak room-temperature strain-rate sensitivity.
The hypothesis ceases to apply if the alloy decomposes into intermetallic or BCC phases.
Yield strength should be strongly strain-rate dependent at 77 K but strain-rate insensitive at room temperature.

contradictions.description: HCP formation is initially described as merely potential and its extent as uncertain, but the falsification rule requires a distinct HCP transformation at 77 K and treats its absence as falsifying the broader glide/twinning hypothesis.

The stacking-fault-energy condition is left as either high or low while being assigned a definite causal role in facilitating twin nucleation, so the proposed boundary condition does not identify a consistent SFE regime.
